A day at sea within the tropics. þÿ We had been several days out, and were bowling along nine knots, with a most lovely little, breeze steady on the quarter. 1 was lounging at my ease under the awning, on a hencoop, reading. It was one of those glorious, fresh, and exhilirating mornings in which it is estacv for a young chap to live, and which arc to be found in noo'her climate under the sun. þÿ Cruise of the Midge.

Bristol. þÿ On Thursday, April 9, Sir Charles Wetherell, the Recorder, entered the city in state, for the firs, time since the fatal disturbances of 1831 þÿ His presence, however, excited no unusual stir. þÿ Among the criminal cases brought before him, was one which is worthy of notice, as an illustration of the fact that the rights of justice, like those of majesty, suffer nothing by the lapse ot time. A woman named Burdock, was accused of having poisoned an aged female, in order to become mistress of her property. The deceased had been buried, and had been suffered to remain in her grave for 14 months, until, suspicions having arisen as to the cause of her death, her body was disinterred, and subjected to examination. The result of various chemical tests applied was, that the stomach contained arsenic. The evidence of a great variety of witnesses having gone to establish the fact of the poison's being administered, But dock was found guilty, and hanged a lew days after.

At tins period 1 had commenced my career as a sailor, and was then lying in a ship of war at Ply mouth under sailing orders for a foreign station, but wailing for a full compliment ol hands þÿ indeed, men were so scarce, that some of the aolest felons had been selected from the jails to make up the crews. AT33. his mother, and bitter recollections crossing his mind, lie threw the þÿboatswain s-mate from him to the opposite side of the deck. This w as considered an act of mutiny, and poor Tom was put in irons, with his legs stapled to the deck. Being, however, a good seaman his services were required þÿ so that lie was shortly afterwards released, and sent to do his duty on the forecastle. We sailed in a few days, and after being some time at sea. the captain remembering what had taken place in harbour, ordered poor Tom, by way of punishment, to perform most of the menial offices of his station, and at length insisted on his executing the most d< grading duty in a ship ot war þÿ that of sweeping the decks. This he refused with a respectful firmness, and in that he w as certainly wrong, for obedience is the first test of þÿduty þÿ no matter from what motive the order proceeds, and in refusing to obey, Tom acted improperly as a seaman þÿ but who can condemn him, hiving the feelings of a man? His refusal, however, was of no avail þÿ the broom was lashed bv small cotds to his hands, and a þÿboatswain mate s stood ready with a ropi þÿ s end to enforce command. Tom obst nateiy declared that he would die rather than submit to unmerited þÿoppression the blows fell heavy on his back, hut they could not change the purpose of the heart. In the moment of his anguish, whilst smarting from the stripes, but writhing still more with inward torture that bowed his spirit, he uttered some dreadful invectives upon the tyranny of his commander.

The hands were immediately turned up, the gratings were seized to the gangway, and poor Tom was ordered to strip for a flogging. Resistance was useless, his outspread arms and extended legs were lashed to the grating, and after reading the Articles of War for disobedience of orders, the captain directed the þÿboatswain s-mate to give him two dozen. This was not the first time that 1 had witnessed punishment at the gangway, for scarcely a day had passed without it since my joining the ship. But poor Tom had been my early friend þÿ I < ailed to mind the happy hours we had passed together, and now to see him w ith his hack lare,crated and bleeding, the eat o'nine tails cutting deep into the flesh þÿ oh, it was too much for me to endure, and I fell at the þÿcaptain f s eet. He spurned me from him, and the first dozen having been given, a fresh þÿboatswain mate s was called to give the second. Tom never flinched þÿ lie re mained as immoveable as a rock, and the only indication of bodily pain, was occasionlv a contraction of the muscles of his face þÿ a deeper and allabsorbing agony seemed to have triumphed over mere corporeal þÿsuffering an agony arising from the desperate struggles of his soul. I looked at the countenances of the men, but the generality seemed to have sunk into a settled apathy, and only a few who had recently joined us from the Barflcur displayed the workings of determined minds. They gazed at each other and tried to catch the sentiments of the crew þÿ and it was plain, that

had a corresponding feeling animated the whole, consequences the most fatal and desperate must have ensued. But the ship's company had not been long together, and mutual distrust prevented an open declaration of discontent. The flogging ceased, and poor Tom was consigned to the master at arms, and his legs once more fixed in the shackles I tried to approach him, hut was prevented by the marine who stood sentinel over him þÿ my attempt was not, however unnoticed, and the unfortunate victim gave me a look, ami even

a smile of grateful acknowledgment. All 1 then my hea' ; sunk within me. 1 retired to the dark recess of the cable tier, and gave vent to my tears þÿ for what could a child in his twelfth year do to save the sullorer from the strong arm of power ? 1 consoled ms self with the idea that Tom would soon he released, but in this too 1 was mistaken þÿ for on the following morning he persisted in his refusal to sweep the decks, was again seized up to the gangway, and two dozen lashes more were inflicted upon his already scored and mangled back. The torture was beyond human endurance, and though no shriek betrayed the anguish of the smart yet a convulsive spasm too clearly indicated the rending of the wounds. Si ill his firmness did not forsake him, and whilst the cal full heavy on his shoulders, he remonstrated with his persecutor, and appealed to the officers whether he had not always performed his duty No voice was raised ill Ins behalf, though looks spoke as forcible as looks could speak, the detestation of every one for such merciless cruelty. At diis moment ill Scott stepped from among the assembled crew þÿ he looked wildis upon his messmate, the Barfleurs þÿ but till remained motionless as statue, and he resumed his station. Again the lash descended, and again the instrument of punishment was stained with the blood of the wretched man. Imprecations on the captain burst from bis lips, and madness seemed to dictate his wild incoherent ravings þÿ he was no longer passive, his mind gave

wav, and at the last stroke lie hung s< useless by the cords which bound his wrists to the grating. He was east lose, and on his reviving, was again shackled in the irons, w ith the promise of a renewal of punishment on the morrow if he still disobeyed. In fact, the captain found bis authority was at sake ; lie saw lie had excited dissatisfaction; he knew that the principal portion of his crew (many of them desperate characters,) were not to lie trusted, and the very men on whom he placed reliance the B.u flours þÿ were disgusted with his treatment. þÿ - þÿ --a RATCUFFE HEROINE IN REAL LIFE. In the year 171(5, a short time before the battle of Culloden, the Castle of , in the north of Scotland, was inhabited by its then proprietor, Captain D þÿ , a young officer of the royal army, and zealously attached to the house of Brunswick ; by his sister, a young lady of a timid disposition and delicate health? and by her particular friend, Miss M þÿ , a daughter of Lord R þÿ , a woman of superior understanding and great resolution, and as much attached to the throne as the proprietor of the castle This castle (now destroyed) was of great extent, and, from the superstition of the natives of the country, had for many years acquired the reputation of being haunted. Captain L) þÿ , who had lately quitted the Duke of Cumberland's army, to which he was shortly, to return, appeared for some time extremely thoughtful ; and one day when his sister was confined to her toom, be told Miss M þÿ he wished to have some private conversation with her, and to entrust her with a secret which had hitherto been carefully preserved in his family, and never disclosed but from father to son, so that never more than two persons had been in possession of it at the same time ; that he would have revealed it to his sister but that he did not think she possessed strength of mind and resolution enough to make the proper use of it ; and as the time was now come when it was necessary for this important secret to be confided to some person besides himself, he entreated her, as a friend to his family, to become the de-

pository of it, and to undertake the necessary engagements attached to the possession of it. Miss M þÿ , unwillingly to bind herself to an undertaking of which she did not know the extent, and in which she found that fortitude was a necesssary qualification, which necessarily implied it might be attended with dangerous consequences, begged to be excused, from a trust of such magnitude as this appeared to be, and wished to decline any further communication on the subject. But Captain I) þÿ was not easily deterred from his purpose, and conjured her. not only from the friendship she professed, and which he knew she had for the family, but if this motive was not sufficiently powerful, by the still more important consideration that the safety, and even the existence, Orthe English army under the Duke of Cumberland must depend on her resolution and exertion, as he knew no one else at this critical moment >n whom he could confide this important secret. Staggered by these forcible arguments, and relying on the well known honour and integrity of Captain þÿD , Miss M- was at length persuaded to give a reluctant consent to her friend's entreaty, and agreed, that, after all the inhabitants of the castle had gone to rest, he should call upon her for the fulfillment of her promise, Accoidingly, about one o'clock in the morning she heard a gentle tap at the door. She was in a trembling expectation of the signal, and leaving the chamber accompanied by Captain D þÿ to the library, where he had provided

two cloaks, in one of which he wrapped Miss M , and throwing the other over his own þÿ shoulder, took a dark lantern which he had prepared, and called to her to summon till jicr resolution, to recollect the vast importance of the duty she had engaged in, and to follow him without fear, as he would lead her into no danger. He then conducted her tip several flights of stairs to a part of the castle she had never been in, and which had never been inhabited in the memory of man. They then

&A3TS& vmwmm&TSL - . þÿ descended into the vaults of the castle, and, mounting another flight of steps, found themselves in a court, which they traversed, Miss M þÿ 's courage so completely failed her in the course of their progress, that she stopped, and once more entreated Captain D þÿ to be relieved from her promise and permitted to return to her apartment, but he urged her to proceed by every argument in his power, and assured her they were almost arrived at the place of their destination, and had no cause for alarm. Ashamed at her own want of resolution, she once more agreed to proceed if the distance was not great. They reached the opposite corner of the court, and arrived at a low door, at the bottom of a turret, which opened with a key with which he was provided. As soon as Miss M þÿ had entered tiiis door, he locked it in the inside, took the key with him, and desired her to observe exactly what be did. He then took her up a narrow winding staircase, at the top of which he unlocked a door, and closed it after them, when tliey found themselves 111 a small square stone chamber, which had only one small window, closed by a shutteropposite the door. In the middle of the floor was a large trap door, to which Captain D þÿ applied a key, unlocked it, and lifted up the trap, beneath which a sort of ladder staircase led to a cha.noer below. He went first with his lantern, and assisted Miss M þÿ to descend ; and when she reached the bottom, he informed her they were now arrived at the place con-

cerning which so much secrecy was necessary ; that in this room, unknown to any one but himself, were concealed all the title deeds, papers, and other effects of value belonging to his family, who, from the distraction of the times, had required such a place of concealment. But this room now contained what was still of more importance ; for the late of the English army depended upon the security of that chamber. The Duke of Cumberland, on bis arrival in Scotland, expressed great anxiety for the large sums he had brought with him for the payment of his troops, and other purposes attending so important a crisis. Captain D þÿ , aware of the security of this place of concealment, offered the use of it, which had stood undiscovered for ages, to his royal highness, who, well aware of his unshaken loyalty, had willingly accepted it and entrusted Captain D þÿ with the concealment of his treasure, from which he would receive weekly supplies without danger or suspicion. Captain D þÿ 's situation in the English army required his presence there ; and it was to be the guardian of this secret, and the keeper of this treasure, for winch he wanted a person of honour and resolution, which induced him to repose his confidence in Miss M þÿ , who, from her residence, with his sister, would excite no suspicion, as the reception of a stranger in the absence of Captain D þÿ might have done. Miss M þÿ aware of the importance of the confidence reposed in her, promised to lulfil her engagement, by descend-

ing alone every Thursday night to take out such sums and orders as might be necessary, and to deliver them next morning to a servant whom Captain D þÿ was to dispatch from the army to convey tlietn to him. This arrangement being made to Captain D þÿ 's satisfaction, and to Miss þÿM 's great anxiety, they returned in the same manner they came, to the habitable part of the castle, Captain D þÿ way accounting for what had happened entreating her to observe exactly what he did in their progress, that she might be sure to proceed in safety. lie re-conducted her to the chamber, delivered to her the key, and alter the most fervent thanks, took his leave,

Avm. and the next morning early departed for the army. Many were the anxious moments to Miss þÿM between the morning, of his departure, and the fatal night in which she felt bound by every tie ol honour and duty to fulfil the engagement she had entered into,- Though a woman of great spirit, and resolution, she was not totally free from that superstition for which her countrymen, notwithstanding their strong sense and informed minds, are so remarkable : and the idea of her solitary expedition at night through the uninhabited parts of this remarkable castle, added to the high importance to the charge with wh cli she was entrusted, weighed heavily on her mind, and rendered her less equal to the task. When the eventful night arrived no fears nor suffering of the mind could deter her from fulfiling, to the best of her power, the engagements she had entered into ; and in the dead of the night, at the time appointed, she left the chamber with the keys, the clonk, and the dark lantern, with which Captain D þÿ had furnished her; with hurried steps, and a palpitating breast she traversed the long passages, mounted and descended the long flights of stairs passed through the vaults, and at Icnglh found herself in the court in which formerly her courage had failed her. She proceeded without a moment's hesitation to the foot of the turret, unlocked the door, and, according to Captain D þÿ 's particular injunctions, locked it in the inside, and, taking the key witli her, went up the winding stair-

case. She unlocked the door, and entered the square stone room; but impatient to complete her task, that she might meet with as few impediments as possible in her return, she did not close and lock the door after her, but left it a little ajar. Finding something particularly close and gloomy in this chamber, she unfastened and opened the w indow, not considering that her light might possibly betray tier. She unlocked and lifted up the trap door, congratulating herself that her task was nearly completed. She descended with her lantern in her hands, and had already proceeded above half the way down, w hen she was alarmed on a sudden by a tremendous noise front the chamber above. The trap door at. the same moment was closed with a thundering clap, and terror so completely overwhelmed her, that the lantern fell from her hand, and she sunk lifeless at the bottom oflhe steps. She was not hurt by the fall, and when she began to recover, she listened attentively if she could hear any footsteps or voices that might in any way account for the cause of her alarm ; but all was still and silent. After waiting for a considerable time, she began to flatter herself that some accidental cause had created those tremendous sounds. She ventured up the ladder, intending, by lifting up the trap door, to re-enter the stone chamber, and, by waiting till day break, endeavour to regain the apartment before the family were stirring. But bow great was her dismay, how unutterable her anguish,

less endeavours, she resigned herself to her fate, and, submittfng unrepining to the will of Providence, all earthly hope was past. This very singular art has given rise to a variety of extraordinary tales ; we coppy the following very amusing one from Dr. John Mason Good's Book of Nature : þÿ The gallant Francis I. of France had an equally gallant and very shrewd valet dechambre, of the name of Lewis Brabant who was also a most skilful ventriloquist. Lewis Brabant had the misfortune to fall desperately in love witli a young, very beautiful, and very wealthy heiress, whose father forbade bis addresses, in consequence of the disparity of his condition. The father, however, died soon after, and the courageous lover, unsubdued by a first repulse, was determined to try his fortune a second time, under favour of the new state of circumstances, and to see whether it would not be possible, under a s -vere push, to c;.li to his aid the art of vent iloquism, in which he was so considerable an adept. He accordingly waited upon the mother as soon as decency would allow, and once more submitted his proposals. But faithful to the views of her deceased husband, the mother of the young lady made no scruple of once more giving Lewis Brabant a direct refusal. þÿ While, however, she was in the act of doing so, a low, hollow, sepulchral voice was heard by herself, and by every friend who was with her, and which was instantly recognised as the voice ol the deceased, commanding her to give her daughter's hand immediately to Lewis Brabant, who the piteous spirit affirmed he now knew to be a most worthy and excellent young man, and considerably wealthier

than he had taken him to lie when alive ; adding, at the same time, that lie was at that mo. ment suffering a part of the pains of purgatory for having ill-treated, by his refusal, so exemplary a man; and that he would not be released from them till his widow had consented. All was mute astonishment ; but Lewis Brabant appeared more astonished than the rest. He modestly observed, that whatever his merits or his virtues might be, lie bad 110 idea that they were worthy of being commemorated by a voice from the grave ; but that nothing could give him more pleasure than to be made the happy instrument of extricating the old gentleman from the pains of purgatory, which it seemed lie was suffering on his account I here was no doubt as to the voice ; and, consequently, there was 110 doubt as to the path to be pursued: the mother, the daughter, the whole family, immediately assented with one accord, and Lewis Brabant had the honor to receive their commands to prepare for the nuptials witli all speed. To prepare for the nuptials, however, required the assistance of a little ready money; but Lewis Brabant was destitute of such an article. It was necessary, nevertheless, to procure it; and he now resolved to try whether the same talent which had obtained for him the promise of a wile, might not also ob tain lor hiin the material he stood in need of. lie lecollected that there lived at I yons an old miserly banker, of the name of Cornu> who had accumulated immense wealth bv

usury and extortion, and whose conscience appeared often to be ill at ease, in consequence of the means he hail made use of; and it immediately struck him that M. Cornu was the very character that might answer his purpose-

To Lyons, therefore, he went instantly post-haste commenced an immediate acquaint ance with M. Cornu, and on every interview took especial care, on entering into conversation witli him, to contrast the pure happiness enjoyed by the man whose conscience c mid look back, like M. Cornu's, as lie was I leased to sav, on a life devoted to acts of charity and benevolence, with the horrors of the wretch who had amassed heaps of wealth by usury and injustice, and whose tormented mind only gave him now a foretaste of what he was to expect hereafter. The miser was perpetually desirous of changing the conversation ; but the more he tried, the more his companion pressed upon him w ith it ; till finding, 011 one occasion, to be t fie golden moment for putting his scheme into execution: and at that instant a low, solemn, sepulchral mutter was heard, as in the former case, which as at last found to be the voice of M. v Cornu's father, who had been dead for some year , and which declared him to have passed all t s time in the torments of purgatory, from which he had just now learned that nothing could free him but his son's paying ten thousand crowns into the hands of Lewis Brabant, then with him, for the purpose of redeeming Christian slaves from the hands of the Turks. All, as in the last case, was unutterable astonishment ; but Lewis Brabant was the most astonished of the two; modestly declared that now for the first time in his life he was convinced of the possibility of the dead

holding conversation witn the living: and admitted that, in truth, he had for many years been benevolently employed in redeeming ! Christian slaves from the Turks, although his native bashfulness would not allow liim to avow it publicly. The mind of the old miser was distracted with a thousand contending passions. He was suspicious without having any satisfactory reason for suspicion : filial duty prompted him to rescue his father from hi abode of misery ; hut ten thousand crowns was a large suin of money even for such a purpose. He at length resolved to adjourn the meeting till the next day, and to change to another place. þÿ He required time to examine into this mysterious affair, and also wished, as he told his companion, to give his father an opportunity of trying whether he could not bargain for a smaller sum Tliey accordingly separated ; but renewed their meeting tile next day with the punctua ity of men of business. The next place made choice of by M. Cornu, for this re-encounter, was a common in the vicinity of Lyons, where there was neither a house, nor wall, nor a tree, nor a bush that could conceal a confe» derate, even if such a person should be in employment. No sooner, however, had they met than the old banker's ears were attain assailed with the same hideous and sepulchral cries, upbraiding him for having suffered his father to remain for four-and-twenty hours longer in all the torment of purgatory; denouncing that, unless the demand of the ten thousand crowns was instantly complied with,

the sum would be doubled ; and the miser himself would be condemned to the same doleful regions, and to an increased degree of torture. M. Cornu moved a few paces forward, but he was assailed with still louder shrieks; lie advanced a second time, and now instead of hearing his father's voice alone, he was as-

mmr. sailed with the dreadful out cry of a hundred ghosts at once, those of his grandfather, his great grandfather, his uncles and aunts, and the whole family of the Cornus for the last two or three generations ; who, it seems, were all equally suffering in purgatory þÿ and were included in the general contract tor the ten thousand crowns : all of them beseeching hiin in the name of every saint in the calendar to have mercy upon them and to have mercy upon himself. It required more fortitude than M. Cornu possessed to resist the threats and out cries of a hundred and fifty or two hunded ghosts at a time. He instantly paid the ten thousands crowns into the hands of Lewis Brabant, and felt some pleasure that by postponing the payment for a day, he had at least been able to rescue the whole family of the Cornu for the same sum of money as was at first demanded for his father alone. The dexterous ventriloquist, having received the money, instantly returned to Paris, married his intended bride, and told the whole story to his sovereign and the court, very much to the entertainment oi all of them. -OOO Information has been received by the packet, that Charles Wood ley, Esq.' the Collector of his Majesty's Customs at this port, and Wm. The late Mrs Hemans. þÿ Felicia Dorothea Browne was born in Liverpool, in a small quaint looking house in St Anne street, now standing, old fashioned and desolate, in the midst of the newer buildings by which it is surrounded. Her father was a native of Ireland, her mother a German lady, a Miss W anner, but descended from, or connected with some Venetion family, a circumstance which she would playfully mention as, accounting for the strong tinge of her romance and poetry which pervaded her character from her earliest childhood. Our abstaining from any attempt minutely to trace her history requires no apology, it is enough to say that when she was very young her family removed from Liverpool to the neighbourhood of St. Asaph, in North Wales; that she married at a very early age, that her married life, after flic birth of five sons, was clouded by the estrangement of her husband, that, on the death of her mother, with whom she had resided, she broke up her establishment in Wales, and removed to Wavertrec, in the neighbourhood of Liverpool, from whence, after a residence of three years, she again removed to Dublin her last resting-place, þÿ Athcnwuin.

WILLIAM CORBET. This powerful and original writer died on Thursday the 18th June, at his farm in Surrey, aged 73. He retained his faculties till the last moment, and died with perfect composure.

3>A»3Ut Y3131Et»l&X3lt jaa«:U3HCk3 ATX3, Cobbett was a self taught man in the true sense of the word, llis father possessed a small piece of ground at Farnham, in Surrey, and Cobbctt himseF was brought up as a common agricultural labourer. In 1783 he quitted his father's roof and repaired to Loudon, where he succeeded in finding employment in the olfice of an attorney. Having enlisted as a common soldier, he was sent to Novo Scotia, and attained the rank of sergeant-major On the return of the regiment to England, he became involved as prosecutor in a-court-martial, but did not await the issue. He left England for France, and sailed from a French port to the United States, where he maintained himself for some time by teaching English to Frenchmen. At that time the French, or democratic party, in America, were loud in their abuse of England' and Cobbett was induced to espouse the cause of his mother country. He published a suc-

of Peter Porcupine, written with great force and vivacity, some of which were reprinted at the time in England, lie was convicted ol a libel against Dr. Rush, and subjected to heavy damages. In 1891 he returned to England and established a morning paper under the title of the Porcupine, in which lie warmly supported Mr. Pitt That paper, however, soon failed, and he soon afterwards set up the Register, which has been continued to the present time. Cobbett commenced bis career as a public writer in England under very favourable circumstances. lie was powerlully patronised by the ministry. Mr. Wynuham went even so far in the House of Commons as to deciare that a statue of gold ought to be erected to htm llis health was drank at Tory dinners throughout the island, llis letters on the subject of the Treaty of Amiens produced a great sensation both here and on the Continent. Of this production it was said by the celebrated Swiss historian, Mullet, that it was more eloquent than any thing that hud appeared since the days of Demosthenes. It is generally understood that Mr. Pitt gave offence in some way to Cobbett : for on his return to power Cobbett lost no opportunity ol attacking his ministry with great bitterness. 01 Mr. Wyndham he long continued to speak favourably, but to him he became also hostile. The President sent his answer in the form of 1 I From a church and king man Cobbett became ) in 1895 a Radical. In 1810 he was sentenced to two years' imprisonment in Newgate,

and a line of 1,999/. From an idea that lie would be deprived of his liberty under an anticipated suspension of the Habeas Corpus On the 27th of July, General Paez entered i Act, he left England lor America in 1817, whence he returned when the suspension tcr- 1 initiated. It had long been a great object ol his ambition to sit in the House ot Commons, and after the passing ol the reform bill he was returned for Uldlium through the influence ol Mr. Fielden, an extensive manufacturer at Todtnorden. As a reasoner, in the proper sense of the word, Cobbett did not rank high, lie never saw the whole of a subject, and his views were, therefore, always partial. But give him a special case, and lie could make more of it than any man. His illustrations were peculiarly forcible, and whatever he had to describe he described well llis"liural Rides" contains, perhaps, the very best descriptions of English scenery that ever were written. His descriptions of rural life in Pennsylvania, when he left England in 1817, arc also admirable. Being an accurate observer, his language was always graphic, llis style was

always racy and idiomatic. In his earlier productions he was somewhat declamatory, and indicated a familiarity with French writers ; as he ad' anced in years his language and style became more Saxon. Though Cobbett upon the w hole was a good speaker, he was not a good debater, and there , fore was not in his element in the House of Commons. He could get on well enough in a lecture, when he had all the talk to himself, but he could not hear opposition with temper, and he had not a command of resources sufficient for the exigencies of a discussion. He has left a widow and a large family two of his sons are at the bar, and are, we believe, exceedingly w ell liked. One of them wrote the well-known description of the turning up ot the Rads, quoted by the Quaiterly Review as one of the happiest of Cobhett's effusions. No man could have occupied the public so constantly with himself as Cobbett has done, without possessing great talents. Take him with all his faults as a writer, and he will still be an extraordinary man.

MM o'ri cats Earthquake atOmoa. þÿ Exlractof a letter, dated, Omoa, February 7, 1835. þÿ The most tremendous irruptions ol valcanoes have taken place in the interior upon record þÿ live burst simultaneously in different places attended witii tremendous earthquakes which sunk three large towns, besides many villages, so that no trace of them remains, and destroyed a large portion of St. Miguel and St. Salvador. The air was so obscured by ashes and smoke, that for eight days the inhabitants were obliged to grope their way with torches. The repoi ts were like the firing of musketry and cannon attended wiih showers of rocks, and stones and cinders. The lava, in some places, rail the distance of sixty leagues, destroying every thing in its course. In Alaneiio they thought the day of judgment had arrived, and more than 3000 marriages took place among the people who had previously lived in a state of concubinage. 1 think a visitation of that kind might be benelicial in New Urleans. þÿ The earthquakes were felt very sensibly botli here and in Truxillo, and the reports of the irruptions a long way to the northward ol Belize. The ashes fell here for about twenty hours like snow, and it was so dark as to require caudles at i2 o'clock A M. One volcano burst about forty miles back of Truxillo. The political state of the country has improved very much since the federation, and from the extreme productiveness of the soil, if things continue permanently in this condition, the country must resume its former vigour. The

government have laid an additional duty of seven per cent on all goods brought from Belize, which if carried into effect will ruin that place and be the making of this. Accounts from the interior state the indigo crop to be very large, and sales have been made in Belize of prime quality at 5 and 6 rials. þÿ Very little, however, is doing at present in any kind of produce, either here or at Truxilloowing principally to the continuance of uie rainy season. þÿ Acic Orleans bulletin.

thunder storm. Bradford was on Wednesday J week attain C visited by one of the most tremendous thunder storms ever witnessed in this part of the country. The three preceding days had been unusually hot and sultry, and on Tuesday thunder was heard rolling at a distance the whole of the afternoon. Wednesday morning was equally hot, and at twelve o'clock thunder was again heard at a distance, which continued without intermission the whole ol the afternoon until six o'clock, when the whole force of the storm burst upon the town. Clap succeeded clap, and Hash followed Hash, with such rapidity as to exhibit one continued roar and blaze which lasted for nearly two hours. In the meantime, hailstones of a verv large size, some measuring from three to four inches, fell in abundance. Much damage was dune to til sky lights in the Exchange Buildings, as well as to the dome of the Court House by the hail. tSome of the hailstones which fell was of an extraordinary size, many being as large as pigeons' eggs þÿ others were three inches in circumfert nee, and resembled pieces of broken icc. The damage done to other windows and sky-lights in the town is incalculable, many thousands of squares having been broken. The lightning also did considerable damage at Pricsthorp, þÿCalverley. 1 he electric fluid descended the chimney of a cottage, occupied by a person named Craven, who was sitting near the fire with his wile

and three of his children : the wife was struck speechless, but soon recovered, ami one of tbe children was struck blind, and lias not yet recovered his sight. At Bramley two cows were killed, one belonging to a poor widow who had little else to support her. A cow belonging to W B. C Stuiidsluld, Esq., of Fs'iolt, was also killed. At Idle the water rose so rapidly as to cause two or three hundred pounds worth of damages to the tan yard of Harrison At Yeadon, a poor woman with a child in her aims was struck d ad but the child received no injury. þÿ Glasgow Courier,

ST. THOMAS AUGUST 1835. On Wednesday night last, the Weather looked threatening, and showed every appearance of a gale, the wind blowing very strong from the East, and N. E. We are however happy to state, that the shipping in the harbour sustained no damage, and with the ex ception of a few old fences blown down, the town received no injury. the king s reply to the lord bishop of jamaica. We are happy in being enabled to state, from undoubted authority, that his Most Gracious Majesty was pleased to express himself very strongly to our revered Diocesan, on the subject of Religion in this Island, upon the occasion of the address to his Majesty by the Prelates of his dominions. llis Majesty, on that day, in the course of his reply, used these words, wiiich were taken down immediately after as accurately as they could be from memory þÿ " there is among the most Revered and Right Reverend Prelates, whom 1 now address, one from a distant part ol my dominions, but with which I happen to be well acquainted, for it was one of the ad vantages of my early education, an advantage denied to most other Princes, to have visited distant parts of the British Empire, and I beg, through the Bishop of Jamaica, to declare my most earnest desire to promote, by every means in my power, in that distant part of my dominions all those blessings of Religion, according to the doctrines of the Established Church, which are enjoyed by my other subjects." The above assurances are most flattering, and amply testily the generous leclings entertained oy his Majesty towards his Colonial dependencies, but particularly in favour of the Island of Jamaica. Such sentiments as are above expressed, cannot but attach the Colonists to their gracious Monarch, and call forth their loyalty and attachment to his person, throne, and government. It is with pleasure we add, that his Lordship the Bishop of Jamaica has received as-

surances o! considerable pecuniary assistance from several Societies for the purpose of promoting the building of Schools an I places of Worship in this Island. Much interest appears to be felt, in general, respecting this Colony. þÿ Royal Gazette .

Mutiny at Sea þÿ A mutiny of a most serious character broke out in the month of November last, on board the bark Manly, Captain John Davis master, while at sea, and which was put down in a most extraordinary manner. The vessel sailed from London on a whaling expedition to the South seas in August last, with a crew of twenty-five men ; but in consequence of the mutiny was obliged to put into Buenos Ayres, from whence she arrived last week in the St. Catherine's Dock, The dissatisfaction of the crew w as originally excited by the captain's refusing them a double allowance of o grog. o On the gist, the stewai d informed the capt. that the crew were only waiting a favourable opportunity to seize the ship. On the 22d the spirits were again refused to the crew, and the captain prepared for the worst, and secretly removed six barrels of gunpowder and 1,500 rounds of catridges into Ins state room, "and then loaded his pistols. At eight, r m , VV h.tc, the chnf otlicer, who it appears, was one of the mutineers, entered the cabin, and was told by the captain that if any attempt was made to take tne ship, he would blow up every soul on board. White advised him not to be rash, and be would stand by him. On Sunday, white told the crcvv the captain would blow up the ship next day it lie did not find land, and they had better secure him. It was afterwards resolved that White should go below and seize the captain, and that, on a given signal, the second and third mates should proceed to his as-

sistance, secure his hands and teet, and throw him overboard The captain having full information of what was going on from the steward, determined rather than the ship should be taken, to perish with all on hoard. After recommending his soul to Gad. he looked up the companion, and obser.ed the three mates, one of whom had a rope in his hand ready to secure him. The captain then, holding the muzzle of one pistol into a barrel of powder, and the other pistol in his right hand, prepared to meet them. White first came down, but appereil thunderstruck when the captain, directing his pistol towards him, declared that if he moved an inch, he would blow his brains out, and discharge the other pistol into the powder. White appeared petrified with fear, and the captain remained in this position several minutes, with the pistol ready cocked, observing the slightest pressure on tiie trigger would send them all in the air. White begged for mercy, and the captain drove him with the muzzle of the pistol into a state-room, where he locked him in. The second mate catne down soon after to look lor White, and on receiving a similar reception, run up the companion and fell against his brother, who was standing on the hatchway þÿ The captain, finding the ship was going out of her course, went on the deck with the steward well armed, and found some of the men inclined to relent, lie threatened to shoot the first man that disobeyed his orders, and restricted the crew to a particular part

of the vessel. Hearing, however, that the crew were still disposed to seize the ship, lie thought it best to run her into Buenos Ayres. There the ringleaders were secured, and they are expected shortly in England for trial. þÿ The conduct of Captain Davies in this trying affair has been spoken of at Lloyd's and in the City as above all praise. The Manly is a lino vessel, and there was every prospect

AV38 of a profitable voyage. She was formerly a fourteen-gun brig, and was well provided with þÿ arms and ammunition, which is supposed to have excited the crew to mutiny, as being well adapted for a piratical expedition. þÿ Atlas.

There are many things which are better left to chance : precaution is sometime more mischievous than negligence. þÿ The late Sir \V C , was one day expected at a large dinner party, at M þÿ d þÿ y's, in Russellsquare. The worthy Baronet's nose, it will be remembered, was, to say the least of it, remarkable. Before the company were assembled, M r. M suggested to his lady, that, upon ibis particular occasion, it would be safer that little Alfred should not (as at other times) be introduced along with the desert after dinner ; for that he, the said Alfred, a fine child, of seven years old, having a propensity to make observations upon all personal delects or deformities, from a pimple to a bump, from crooked finger to a cork leg, might possibly say something not altogether agreeable to .Sir VV , " Leave that to me,'' said the lady ; " I'll contrive it nicely." Accordingly she proceeded to the nursery, and thus addressed the little gentleman : þÿ " Alfred my dear, we have a gentleman coming to dinner to day who has a monstrous ugly nose. Now, if you will promise to be a very good boy, and not make any observations upon it,you may come down after dinner, and shall have an orange. But, remember the nose ! Master Alfred acceded to the terms of the" treat, and, in due time, was ushered into tho dinner-room. After the lapse of a quarter of an hour, the young gentleman, finding the re ward of his forbearance still in arrear, took advantage of a dead pause in the conversation,
and cried out from the further end of the table, " Mama, is it time now for me to have the orange you promised me, if I didn't say any thing about that gentleman's monstrous ugly nose ?"

THE SPERM WHALE. The Sperm Whale is subject to several diseases, one of which is a perfect or imperfeet loss of sight. A whale, perfectly blind, was taken by Captain W Swain, now of the Sarah and Elizabeth whaler, of London, both eyes of which were completely disorganized, the orbits being occupied by fungous masses, protruding considerably, rendering it certain that the whale must have been deprived of vision for a long space of time, yet, notwithstanding this, the animal was quite as fat, and produced as much oil, as any other captured of the same size. Besides blindness, the whale is frequently subject to deformity of the lower jaw, two instances of which 1 have seen myself, in which the deformity was so great as to render it impossible for the animal to find the jaws useful in catching small fish, or even one might have supposed in deglutition. Yet these whales possessed as much blubber and were as rich in oil, as any of a similar size 1 have seen before or since. # # þÿ Old whalers affirm that it is caused by fighting ; thev state that the sperm whale fights, by rushing, head first, one upon the other, their mouths at the same time wide open, their object, appearing to he the seizing of their opponent by the lower jaw, for which purpose t i icy frequently turn themselves on their side; in this manner they become, as it were locked together, their jaws crossing each other, and in this posture they strive vehemently for the mastery ; 1 have never had the good fortune to w'itness one of these combats ; hut if it be

the fact that such take place (of which 1 have little doubt), we need not wonder at seeing so many deformed jaws in this kind of whale, for we can easily suppose the enormous force exerted on these occasions, taking into consideration, at the same tune, the comparative slenderness of the jaw bone in this animal. þÿ Some corroboration of the above statement arises from the fact, as far as my knowledge extends, that the female is seldom or never seen affected wiih this deformity. Erom these facts it may almost be deduced or at least surmised, with a great degree of probability that the mode of procuring food, as above stated, as that pursued by the sperm whale, is the true one ; for without eyes, and with a jaw (his only instrument of prehension) so much deformed, the animal would seem to be incapable of pursuing his prey, and would consequently gain but very precarious sub- a sistence, if his food did not actually throng about the mouth and throat, invited by their appearance, and attracted also, as some suppose, by the peculiar and very strong odour of the sperm whale. It is a well known fact, that many kinds of fish are attracted by substances possessing a white dazzling appearance ; for not only the hungry shark, but the cautious and active dolphin, both occasionally fall victims to this partiality, as 1 have had many opportunities of observing. When the Kent, South Sea whaler, was fishing on the < off shore ground of þÿPeru, the crew caught a great number of the sepia octopedia, or

squid (the peculiar food of the sperm whale) in one night, by merely lowering a piece of polished lead, armed with fish hooks, a certain depth in the sea. The sepia gathered around it instantly, so that by giving a slight jerk to the line, the hooks were easily driven into their bodies. The teeth of the sperm whale are merely organs of prehension, they can be of no use for mastication, and, consequently, we find that the fish, Ac., which he occasionally vomits, present no marks of hav.

The rise of the water in the //arbour is a remarkable feature in the late storm It began early in the afternoon, and increased gradually, but not entirely unobserved by near residents and others concerned in small Cratts, for several who had boats drew them up on the wharves. As the evening advanced it rose six feet above the level of the piers. A large heavy raft of Mr Ashford's 30 feet long which had been hauled up for Six Months before, and had a yawl lashed to it, were floated off' and have never since been heard of; several boats floated high up in the Streets and many cellars of the Stores, some an hundred feel from the landing were filled from the sea. The -Sea rose in Parham //arbor eight feet beyond its usual level Without particularizing for the present the variations of the Mercury in the Barometer during the //urricane, we think it will be most generally intelligible to say that it fell one inch and a half. A very sensitive Barometer in the country fell to 28 54.

Effects of the Storm at the Naval Yard and liidge. NAVAL YARD Within the Yard, the Buildings except the Office have been injured in the roofs, door and window shutters. The Sail Loft damaged greatly, one entire side and half the roof blown down. Part of the roof of the Western Capstan House stript of Shingles, the Columns Balast rade of the 1 Vindwiird Caller)/ of aud A 'bian llouss, (Officers Quarters) blown down. The roof and one end of the House occupied by the Officer in charge, and several shutters much damaged. Outside the Yard, the Mast House has been totally destroyed. The windward part of the Gallery of the Commissioner s House partly blown away and several of the out-Offices destroyed : all the other Buildings belonging to the A aval Department arc destroyed, a great many Kitchens, fences, &e. blown down. The only Ships in port were the Steam Packet F/amnr, and the Dutch Brig of War Echo. The Earner was alongside the Eastern Wharf, and has damaged one of her Paddie Wheels, nothing mere. The Echo was moored with three Cables and a Chain þÿ she was driven with such violence as to break two of the Cables and snap the Chain, and dragged tie remaining Cable and Anchor atter her until she came into shallow water near the Office, where site now remains 4) deep in mud ; it doos not appear that she has suffered any injury except the loss of Cables and Anchor which perhaps will be recovered. It is feared there will be much difficulty in getting her out of her bed of mud. All her Guns and Stores have been landed and her Water started to lighten her,
great purchases have been employed to move her, but she has not started yet.

FROAI THE HARBOR MASTER. August 17, 1835. The Sloop Rebecca arrived last evening left St. Bartholomew's on Friday last, several Houses were blown down at that Island. On her way up she touched at Nevis and St. Kilt's -considerable damage was done at both Islands and all the Shipping that could not get under weigh were driven on shore Great anxiety is felt for Captain Balston, and Mr. Isaac Walter, who, in a small Sloop called the Mary Ann, sailed from St. Bart's on Wednesday afternoon, for this Island. The Schooner Doddinglon also, which left Barbuda for this Town on Wednesday forenoon has not yet arrived :-while writing this we are informed that part of one of her sails, the gaff and boom have been picked up by a fishing Boat and brought anu lodged at Mr. Wyke's store.

Through the politeness of a Gentleman in this Town, we have been favored with the loan of '/'he St. Christopher Gazette," dated " 1 4th August, containing an account of the Gale, which occurred in that Island on the 12th instant : part of which, is as follows : þÿ THE GALE : One of those periodical tornados, which at this season of the year the inhabitants of the Antilles are always apprehensive of experiencing, occurred here on Wednesday night last ; which for its severity during the time it lasted, and its devastating effects, has not been exceeded for many years- -indeed, it is the general was opinion, which so very severe, was mild compar- that the //urricane of 1819, ed to that which it is our painful task this day to its ravages all except record, and which it is thought the " Great surpasses in Hurricane" of 1772. The wind, which on Wednesday forenoon was Northerly, began to increase early iu the evening, and between 8 and 9 o'clock blew with great violence from that quarter ; and þÿcontinued changing from N. to N E., and East, until near 12 o'clock, when it shifted to the 8 , and began gradually to abate þÿ during which period, above three hours, the havoc it occasioned is immense ; destroying in Basseterre almost the whole of the small tenements in Irish and New Towns, and the other parts of this metropolis, occupied by the poorer classes ; and injuring, in many instances, large Dwellings, by unroofing "them, removing others from their foundations, and stripping of shingles, Cap-boards, &c. The Wife. By Washington Irving. 1 have often had occasion to remark the lortilude with winch women sustain the most overwhelming reverses of fortune. I hose disasters which break down the spirit of man, and |iiostiate him in the dust, seem to call forth all the energies of ihe suiter sex, and give such intrepidity to their character, that at times it approaches to suhiimily Aothing can be more touching than to behold a soft and tender ltmalo, who had been all weakness and dependence, and alive to every trivial roughness, wlnlc treading the prosperous paths ol life, suddenly rising in menial force to be the comforter and supporter of her husband, under mislortuuc, and abiding with unshrinking firmness the most hitter blasts ol adversity. As the vine which lias long twined its graceful foliage and been lilted by it into sunshine will, when the hardy plant is rivtd by the thunderbolt, cling around it with

.soras. its caressing tendrils, and bind up its shatter, ed houghs ; so it is beautifully ordained by Providence, that woman who is the mere dependant and ornament of man in his happier hours, should be his stay and solace, when smitten with sudden calamity; winding herself into the rugged recesses of his naturet tenderly supporting the drooping head, and binding up the broken heart. I was once congratulating a friend, who had around him a blooming family, knit together in the strongest atlection. þÿ 1 can wish you no better þÿlot, said he with enthusiasm þÿ than to have a wife and þÿchildren. If you are prosperous they are to share in your prosperity ; il otherw ise they are to comfort þÿyou. And indeed 1 have observed, that a married man tailing into misfortune, is more apt to retrieve his situation in the world than a single one ; partly because he is more stimulated to exertion by the necessities of the helpless and beloved beings who depend upon him for subsistence ; but ciuelly because bis spirits are soothed and relieved by domestic endearments, and his sell respect kepi alive by finding that though ail abroad is darkness and humiliation, yet there is still a little world of love at home, of which he is the monarch. Whereas a single man is apt to run to waste and self neglect 5 to fancy himself lonely and abandoned, and his heart to tail to ruin like some deserted mansion lor want of an inhabitant.

Dentistry. Doctor Cross, DENTAL SURGEON, from St. Thomas. Respectfully informs the Ladies and Gentlemen of St. Croix, that he has received permission from the Government to practice the Dental art in this Island. He will insert elegant Artificial and Natural teeth on the roots or gums as the case may require, answering in many instances all the purposes of the original ones. Gangrene of the teeth removed, and decayed ones rendered useful for life by filling with Gold, &c Teeth cleaned and rendered pearly white without the least pain. Tartar of the teeth removed and with it the attending bad breath. Troublesome teeth and old roots extracted with care and safety. Rooms at Miss GILBERTS, Christiansted. Ladies attended at their residences if required The most respectable references given if required. November 9th, 1835.

The capitation tax to the royal treasury is Risk. W. C. for each town negro and Ps. 1 32s k. for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps. 1 for each town negro and 1's. 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus: Capitation tax not amounting

to Ps 20 immediately on taking up the list, but if Ps. 20 and above tha sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance ol the 11th November 1770. That negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly specified in the lists delivered. þÿ All oilier negroes are taxable, including invalids. Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to he delivered to the commissioners. In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 2<>th of September 1833 is to be attended to; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with all the Inhabitants names without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For tin; convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Christiaustrcd and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils lncassator ollicc and in Frederikstird and its Jurisdiction at the police office in that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such in writing to the commission to prevent any. doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further di-

rected, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose to come forward with sullicient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol. It is to be observed that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes and every column properly tilled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their houses, as in such cases it will be considered sullicient when they announce themselves as such together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners.

Distressing Shipwreck. þÿ The brig Mexican, Trussel, of and from this port, lor Eastport and Lnbec, was wrecked on Thursday night, 1st October on Fisherman's Island, and aii but one of the crew perished. During the night the wind blew heavy from the westward, with rain, and about 1 o'clock breakers were discovered ahead. Endeavors were made to haul her by the wind and fetch out to sea, but she immediately struck a ledge, arid soon beat over. Both anchors were then let go, but they broke, and she was drifting upon other breakers, þÿ and seeing no chance lor their lives, the crew (five in all) took to the boat and endeavored to get under lee of Fisherman's Island. After having rowed one mile among the breakers, the boat filled and capsized, and the captain, mate, and two men perished ; the other succeeded in holding on to the boat, and the next morning was taken up on Seal's Island, almost in a state of inscn sibility. þÿ Griggs' Boston bulletin.

The Duke of Nemours. þÿ His Koya I Highness has just arrived, having been granted permission by the King his father, to visit this country for 6 weeks or two months, never having been in England before The Duke will remain, it is expected, a fortnight at Giillion's, and then depart on a short tour to Batln Cheltenham, &c. The Duke of Nemours is described as of very elegant and engaging
manners, and prepossessing person. lie is an excellent linguist, and speaks English with fluency. He intends to make a tour of the country before he returns to France. þÿ London Taper, August 28.

Supposed Pirate þÿ On Sunday, the Bcthen, M'Neil, arrived at Greenock. On the 7th July, in lat. 31. 25. N, long. 63. 37. W., about one in the afternoon, a suspicious-looking schooner was observed astern, which during daylight appeared to gain very little upon the Bi'thea ; but when evening began to set in site came up very fast, and in a short time she was along the weather side. She hailed them, and demanded, first in Spanish, then in French, and lastly in English, from whence they were, and whither they were bound. They were answered "from Demerara to Greenock," and similar questions were put to them, The stranger replied, from Porto Rico, bound to Heligoland She then sailed right across the bows of the Bethea, and fell to leeward where she hove to for about twenty minutes, and appeared as if preparing for action, or getting out boats and preparing for b >urdieg She then made sail, and went fast to windward lor about two miles, during which time those on board the Bethea watched her motions with great anxiety. She next squared her fore-yard and bore away to get in the Bethea's wake, a motion which much increased the suspicions of the captain and crew ol the latter. She came up so rlose þÿ that her jib-boom almost touched the taffrail, and then fell in close along the lee-side, and asked the longitude and some other questions# At this time those in the Bcthen had a good opportunity of examining her appearance þÿ H ;r hull was long and low, with breadth in proportion, vorv taunt masts, with square

yards and large sails, and would register about one hundred tons. I lor decks w ere crowded with people, and she had a large gun placed a midship, with a lantern lighted. Alter looking all round the Bethea, she made sail, and was shortly out of sight. Next moining she was observed to windward, hovering close bv a square-rigged vessel The above particulars were taken from the log. book ot the Bclhea. þÿ Caledonian Mercury.

The oldest inhabitant of this Island, we should imagine, cannot recollect to have seen such a flood of rain as fell during the night of Sunday last, and in the morning of Monday. It is impossible to describe the violence w ith which the torrents of water came dow n upon us. We never heard such rain. In the course of eight hours there was more water on the ground than has been ever seen in that period of time. In October 1819 the flood was t re rnendous, but it had rained without intermission for three days. It was most providential that the rain of Sunday night fell in such alarming torrents only over the parishes of St. Michael, St. George. Christ Church, and St. Philip. A great mercy it was that it did not rain to such an extent on the lands below the bills of St. Andrew «nd St. Joseph; if it had, the consequences would, probably, h#ve been dreadful. Large tracts of land in the valley f St. George are under water, in some places, we understand, the tops only of the canes could be seen on Monday. Places of resort for Invalids. Messrs. Editors, þÿ As the season is fust approaching, when it is necessary as well as customary for such Invalids as are not from the nature of their maladies, able to withstand the rigors of our winter season, to leave their homes and seek a climate more friendly to their þÿshatter constitutions, d 1 deem it my duty as a friend to suffering humanity, to add my mite towards rendering the situation of such as comfortable as circumstances will admit. Most Physicians as well as patients are quite ignorant of the nature of the climates and accommodations of the various places in which Invalids are usually recommended to spend the winter. I know full well that almost every one is acquainted with the climate of the different latitudes, but we would here particularly allude to that of the different Islands and places. For instance, in a general way it well known that the climate of the West Indies is warm and equable, with plenty of sea air &e. Are., and highly salubrious ; but then they do not know that the climate of the various Islands, differs as much in many respects as that of our city from the interior of the State, and every New-Yorker who is at all acquainted with his own State, knows how different the two are. And it. is equally so in the several Islands of the West ladies. In one you will have much of a moist air, in another the reverse, in the third the two combined, and so on with great variety. Again in regard to accommodations (which to an Invalid are almost

if not quite of equal importance with climate,) in some of the Islands, where the climate might be considered such a- is desirable, there are no accomodations, or but extremely indifferent and inconvenient, with bad roads, and added thereto no conveniences for exercise, even on such as arc tolerably good ; so that in recommending one in ill health to go to the West Indies (which we unhesitatingly say to he without exception the best of all places,) a Phvsician or other person scarcely knows which of the chain of Islands to recommend. Perchance he is influenced by some one person to go to this one, because be or some of his friends has derived advantages from going there; and perhaps being ignorant of any other place, he recommends this with all the confidence that such want of information is apt to cause , or his Physician may suggest to him to go here or go there, because fie is in some decree obliged to recommend some situation, without at the same time having any definite idea of that which he recommends. Now for our part we esteem the separation of an In- J valid (the result of whose disease is in most cases uncertain,) from his home, family and friends, and the many little endearments by which we are all attached even in health, to our family circles, as a matter altogether of too much importance to he so lightly treated of as it is usually. And therefore, in hopes of rendering some little assistance to those who are inquiring as to where & when to go, call our remarks upon their attention, and we trust upon

vour well known readiness to communicate to the public aught that is useful, to give a place in your paper lor this communication. In the first place we would remark, in comment upon the expression in the above, (that Physicians are obliged to recommend some situation without having any definite idea of its climate and accommodations,) that this ex- 1 he profession, (for pression arose not from the writer a desire to censure hereof has the honour of being one of its members,) but rather to speak the truth ; as it is well known among them that much more definite information is wanting, and has for a long time been wanting in this mutter. Wc labored under this dilliculty last Fall, and it was after much wavering, that we were enabled to make up our minds where to go. Even in consultation with one of our most eminent and useful Physicians upon this subject, he was unable to direct us definitely except from hearsay ; and thus were wc left to grope our way. But wc must hold that a kind and unerring

Providence directed us to that which proved in all respects to be the best. We will not in this place enter into areview of the advantages and disadvantages of tlie various winter resort for Invalids ; for we do not think it necessary at present, or that it would be interesting to readers in general. Besides also, we do not consider it proper for a newspaper communication, and to the profession we would say that if time and opportunity afford, we may one day, indite them a small epistle, through a Medical Journal, the proper channel for such things. In a general way we may enumerate the different places as far as our memory will serve, at least the following are the most famous, Comment ing at the Virginia Springs þÿ Charleston þÿ different parts of Georgia þÿ Florida, bile þÿ particularly the þÿ Ivey West famous St. Augustine Mo- New Orleans þÿ þÿCuba þÿ Bermuda þÿ Porto Bico þÿ St Thomas þÿ St. Croix þÿ the English and French West India Islands, Curacoa, and the Spanish Main in general þÿ Madeira þÿ and last, and perhaps least, the south of France and Italy. Of all this list there are few indeed that offer advantages to Invalids money superior remaining home, saving so- and to enjoying the at gieat blessing of their cial converse with their families, and the many religious privileges with which we are surrounded, in our highly þÿfavor dland. þÿ We know not that there are among these, in truth and justice to all parties, more than two places that are deserving of notice. St. Au-

gustine, Madeira and Italy are the most iamous ; but we will venture to affirm that where one person, particularly if consumptive, is benefitted, from þÿ, t i o 5 derive no advantage or are injured. W e have been told by one who resided in Madeira for some time, that a common expression when English invalids arrive there is, here comes another to dwell in the orange grove, (the burial place for strangers.) How very consoling ! Madeira possesses many, very many advantages, and also many disadvantages, and so of the other two places, but they are not equal to the former, Italy is not much to be recommended, if wc may trust what that close and great observer (Dr. James i it, and believing that many may not l ave Johnston) says of it in bis work on change of air, also corroborated by many others ; and the writer of this was companion to a gentleman (a Physician,) who passed one winter in that place, and who modestly remarked, it is no place for invalids. The same may be applied to the south of France. St. Augustine has in this country as great a reputation as Madeira and Italy generally have in England and France : but we arc bold to say from much information, principally derived from Physicians who have resided there, for the purpose of improving theii health, that its reputation is founded on a false basis ; and it deserves to rank on the same level wc give to the former places. We have never been there, but were so well satisfied in relation to it, that we were deterred from visiting it last winter, and

have since taken some pains to gain all the j information that canto within our reach. We have just been informed that a Physician of much eminence, of this city, sailed last week for the West Indies, (the Island which we purpose noticing directly) who spent the last winter, which was, we admit, a very unfavorable one, in St. Augustine, and his opinion is adverse to the salubrity of that place, þÿ the general expression of those medical gentlemen with whom we have conversed. One more remark is necessary. It is to lie understood that we do not speak of what these places were, hut what they now are ; for it is well known to most persons, and we have frequently heard the remark made by old residents of the West Indies, that the climate of the different Islands &c. undergoes a great change in the course of 20 or 30 years, so that the one we may now recommend, will not perhaps in that period he at all calculated to benefit those visiting it ; at least, 20 years ago it was not. þÿ'I he question will now naturally suggest itself to the minds of those interested, since vou have passed judgement thus unequivocally upon these the most famous resorts, where would you have us to go l Our answer is, go were we went, and you wdl undoubtedly obtain as great, if not a greater combination

of requisites than can probably he obtained it any other place. þÿDon dear t reader, understand us to recommend to you a specific hut only such a situation as will do you all the good that climate, accommodate >ns, exeivi , scenery and many other good things, can possibly effect. We have before stated it to be our op; r. ion that the West Indies doubtless oiler the most advantages ty the seekers of that treacherous blessing, Health, and also stated that the bain of Islands composing the Indies, though possessing in common, general qualities, yet difþÿfer d materially in themselves, and it therefore behooves us now to mention which link of the chain we would recommend : and in compliance we will say that as lor climate and accommodation there is not one that can claim any very high encomiums from us as a permanent (so to speak for the season) residence ; but upon reference to a map of the West Indies, in about Eat. 17 deg. 45 rn. and Long. 61 deg. 51 m. a little S. Places of resort for Invalids. (continued from our last.) The Island is under Danish Government, and the present Governor-General von Scholten is in all respects very kind and attentive to the comfort and convenience of strangers, (particularly Americans) ; every facility is allbrded at the Custom-House and other public offices, so as to render all things as easy as the duties of the various government officers admit, and the writer has never heard a murmur or complaint by any one (but much rather praise) at the treatment received from those officers. Tiie hospitality and kindness to strangers of the Danes is proverbial, and the Danish residents of this Island fulfil the proverb to the letter. Most of the inhabitants speak the English language. There are also several American merchants established there, whose houses and arms are ever open to receive their countrymen, and who take delight in conferring favouis upon all such, at least so we found it, and we believe the same is the opinion of all who resided there the last winter In the West end of the island, to which we in every respect give all preference as the permanent residence, are two excellent private boarding houses, conducted one by an American lady Mrs. Boyle, and the other by the wife of an American gentleman Mrs. 11. Codwisc, specially designed for the accommodation of the sick and their companions, in which will be found every thing the place will supply. The two houses are differently situated þÿ one is upon a level with the town,

which is btit s nail þÿ just on the northern border þÿ the other a raised ground, but of easy ascent and on the southern border þÿ both well located, fine large houses, standing unconnected with other buildings, and but a few hundred yards from the sea shore, commanding line views of the shipping, the sea, with the surrounding parts of tiie country. They are in all respects well conducted, and invariably afford every satisfaction. We boarded in the lower house kept by Mrs. Codvvise , and from the experience we had of the kindness and attention of herself and family we would thus bear our humble and public testimony; at the same time not wishing to make any distinction between the two houses as both ladies are very attentive, and make it their pleasure to serve the interests and welfare of their boarders. Besides these, there are several private families ready and willing to receive such boarders as prefer this manner of living, and again should any one, or more persons desire it, they generally can hire a house and servants, and thus be entirely private, at very moderate expense. Another great desideratum, at least we, although Physicians, found it so to be, is the attendance if required of able, enlightened, and practical Physicians. To the profession it will be useless to say aught in favour of Danish Physicians, for the school at Copenhagen is ever able to speak for itself, and Doctors are not made therewith that speed and carelessness they arc in many parts of the

world, but only after patient and laborious study Besides, the gentlemen resident at the West End arc men of much experience, and an honor to their profession if we may be allowed to judge. Their charges are ever in proportion to the abilities of the patient to pay. Society is very good ; and what was both pleasing and some what unexpected, from erroneous impressions. Temperance in eating and drinking is conspicuous in all parts. In this important item the Governor General, much to bis credit and honor, sets a noble example. Religious privileges are not perhaps so ample as we would desire to see At enjoy, there being but one English church in that part, and but one Clergyman, whose duties are divided between the two towns. There is a Danish Lutheran and a Moravian church also, but in those the English language is not used. The facilities of communication with the Island of Jit Thomas, which is the port lor vessels from

uuuub' .x -1ki all parts of the States and England, are sufficiently great for those desiring it, to take passage to either of those places : or by means of a Steam Packet which plies regularly every fortnight to most of the Windward and Beeward Islands. This latter is a trip we would lecommend to all who can aflord it, (as the price of passage is very reasonable,) and with whom a sea voyage agrees, recollecting however to make St. Croix their home. We would here advise all going to St. Croix to be sure to embark for the West end of the Island, direct if convenient. Facilities lor exercise are likewise in a measure ample ; particularly should the visiter take his own horse and some light covered vehicle with him, which we would also recommend by all means; and such as do not, will generally obtain ponies of easy gait, and some vehicles, by the month; at very moderate prices. The roads are certainly good as as can be, in most cases being as compact and smooth as flag stone walks in our City, and yet many are soft and much like our country roads, saving you never see a hole or a rut in them. The scenery is beautifully diversified. It is true you do not see much else but sugar cane, and that to the very top of the highest mountains, hills, and dales. Here the eye may rest till wearied on mountains rising on mountains, and then may be cast down and find relief on the level plain, or the broad expanse of waters as smooth and placid as the glittering lake. There are several most beautiful rides, either along the sea

shore tor the distance of five miles, and here at one time you are riding on the top of a hill some 40 or 50 feet above the sea, and in a little you have the waves dashing and foaming at your feet. The whole of this road Or is lined on both sides with cocoa nut trees. you may dip a little into the country, and tor nearly the same distance ride between high and beautiiul mountains either in a vehicle or on horseback, or again you may go from town to town, a distance of 15 miles, on a smooth, and for several miles perfectly level road þÿ Besides, there are several by-ways, all of which constitute a pleasing and necessary variety to the Invalid, as riding is his principal occupation. Further, in general but there a variety and abundance ol fruit, which is was said to be scarce during the last season, and yet there seemed to be a plenty, with which the tables are abundantly supplied. þÿ From the ample rains they have had this summer, fruit promises much better. In conclusion there is an abundance of the good things of this life for any moderate and reasonable man. As we have often remarked, a kind Providence has here provided as great a combination (A requisites lor the service of the sick, as can be found to exist in any one place in the habitable globe. Remember we do not promise that a man shall find a paradise here wherein to rest him, for it partakes of the nature of all sublunary places and things, in having is the a bitter com- the sweet, but we repeat here great with

bination of requisites. We have ttius spoken ol things as we lound them, and if any ol our readers find here aught that is exaggerated or untrue, we will feel much indebted to them for their correction, as truth is our design, and what we solicit. There have already several persons gone within two or three weeks lor tSt. Croix, which is quite unusual so early in the season, but we would recommend to all that can, to go before the lstol .November, and to provide themselves with United Slates passports, as they will find a great convenience m having them.
