The following whimsical circumstance happened some time ago in Kilkenny : þÿ A tailor, who was married to a very sickly woman, grew enamoured of a youg girl who lived in his neighbourhood, and on certain conditions he agreed to give her a promise in writing to marry her immediately on the demise of his wife ; in consequence of which Mr. Snip passed the following curious note of hand ; þÿ " In two days after the demise of my present wife, I promise to marry Miss Moran on okdek, value received, under fifty pounds sterling. Given under my hand this sixteenth day of May, Ate., J. Sullivan." Shortly after Miss Moran received the above note, she died, leaving it endorsed to a female friend, who also chanced to take a fever, and died before the tailor's wife ; however, on her sick bed, she also endorsed the note, and gave it to her cousin, whom the tailor absolutely married, agreeably to the endorsement, in two days after the death of his wife, and the tailot and his wife are now living happily in the city of Kilkenny. þÿ Bell's Life in London.

A Great Speculation. þÿ A gentleman of tilt bar, in a neighbouring county, in easy circumstances and pretty good practice, had rendered himself somewhat remarkable by his attempts in the way of matrimonial speculation A maiden, rather advanced in years, residing some miles distant in the neighbourhood, hearing of the lawyer's speculating propensity þÿ that his character was unexceptionable, and his situation in life tolerably good þÿ resolved upon making him her husband She hit upon the following expedient þÿ she pretended suddenly to bo taken very ill, and sent for the man of law to draw her will. He attended for that purpose. By her will she devised 10,000 dollars in bank stock, to be divided among her three cousins þÿ some thousands in bonds and notes to a niece þÿ and a vast landed estate to a favourite nephew. þÿ The will being finished, she gave the lawyer a very liberal fee, and enjoined secrecy upon him for pretended purposes þÿ thus precluding him from an enquiry into her real circumstances. Need I mention the result ? In a fortnight the lady thought proper to be again restored to health. The lawyer called to congratulate her on her restoration þÿ begged permission to visit her which was politelv given. After a short courtship, the desired offer was made. Hie bargain was concluded, and ratified by the priest. The lawyer's whole estate by his wife consists of an annuity of sixty five þÿdollars. þÿ Western paper.

ANOTHER "INFERNAL MACHINE." On Sunday night, between eleven o'clock, the inhabitants ol Manchester-square were thrown into a state ol the greatest alarm and consternation in consequence of aloud report, similar to that produced by the firing of an immense piece of ordnance. It appears that at the time in question, us an elderly female, named Alary Wilson, residing in Marylebone lane, was proceeding through the square towards home, she observed on the railing in front of the French ambassador's (Count Sebastiain's) residence, a faint glimmering light which she at the time took no particular notice ol, imagining it to be nothing more than the reflection oi a candle in the area. or part of a lighted cigar, which she concluded might have been thrown down by some gentleman in his progress along ; she, however, had not got many yards before she heard a tremendous report, and before she had time to ascertain, by looking round from whence the sound proceeded she was struck on the hack part of the neck w ith a stone, or some other missile, which inflicted on her a wound from which the blood flowed in a stream. At this moment a horse attached to u cub, alarmed by the sound, started off at full speed and galloped at a fearful rate through several streets, but was at length stopped in Oxford street, after knocking down and severely injuring a journeyman carpenter, named Evans, who sprang forward at the risk of his life and seized the animal by the head. By this time an immense number of persons had eongte-

gated Manchester-square, consequence, in in of a report which was freely circulated, that an infernal machine had been fired off with the intention of inflicting personal injury on the ambassador. Police constable Powell, 10!t I), was the first constable on the spot, and on examination of the premises lie diseoNcrod a large hand grenade tied to the railing of Count Sebastiani's residence. It hud evidently been recently fired off, and part of the combustible material was then burning. þÿ It has since been ascertained that two men who had the appearance of foreigners stopped a woman who was walking along the square w ith a lantern, soon after ten o'clock, and that one of them lighted a small piece of candle, which lie put into his hat, remarking to his companion, " It's all right now," w hen they both proceeded on. The affair, following as it has done so closely upon the heels ol the diabolical attempt ol Ficschi, lias created no inconsiderable sensation, and the police arc using their best endeavours to trace out the perpetrators ol the deed. þÿ The Barbadian October 31st, 1835.

3DAHPW> BIKMBSTOOIWfc -»OCOCv«- Effect of Music on Elephants. þÿ Of all animals, man alone excepted, the elephant is the most susceptible of musical sounds. Pliny, Plutarch, Suetonius, and Buffoii, record singular anecdotes of the fondness of this half reasoning quadruped for music ; and we shall conclude the subject with an unique account of a concert which was given to two elephants, in Paris, ISOti or 7. The orchestra was placed above in a gallery, with a trap door in the floor to permit the sound to escape downward. This took place in the Botanic Gardens, and excited great curiosity. All the influence and wealth of Paris were present. On the first sounds of the music, the elephants, which were male and female, and called Hans and Mess, walked around the enclosure þÿ then directed their trunks to the trap door, raising themselves on their hind legs. They now appeared alarmed, but after a few seconds resumed their usual calmness, and abandoned themselves to the delights which the music afforded them. The air was then changed, and one of a savage and rude nature was substituted, and that music possessed influence over them was immediately evident. They approached the bars of the cage, twisted them with their trunks, and pushed against them violently with their bodies þÿ they exhibited symptoms of pain and rage þÿ they seemed to be acting under the influence of some agent over which they had no control.
